title: The LORD Calls Samuel
summary: At a time when the word of the LORD was rare, the boy Samuel, sleeping near the ark at Shiloh, hears a voice calling his name. Three times he runs to Eli, until the old priest realizes the LORD is calling and teaches him to answer. The LORD tells Samuel that the judgment on Eli's house is about to fall; the next morning Samuel reluctantly tells Eli everything, and Eli accepts it. Samuel grows, and all Israel recognizes him as a prophet.
story: Chapter 2 ended with a man of God announcing the downfall of Eli's house. Chapter 3 confirms that word through a new voice and marks a turning point: God is speaking again, and he has chosen a child to speak through. The chapter opens with the word of the LORD rare and closes with the LORD revealing himself at Shiloh by his word. Between those two notes, the leadership of Israel's spiritual life passes from the aging priest to the young prophet. This matters for the whole book, because Samuel will be the one who anoints Saul and David and who speaks God's word to kings. The disaster of chapter 4 follows immediately.
historical:
The setting is still the sanctuary at Shiloh in the last years of Eli, during the eleventh century BC. The phrase from Dan to Beersheba (verse 20) names the traditional northern and southern limits of Israel's settled land, roughly 150 miles apart, and becomes a standard way of saying the whole country. It shows that Samuel's reputation spread beyond his own tribe to all Israel, which prepares for his role as a national leader.

The period of the judges had seen few prophets. Deborah is called a prophetess (Judges 4:4), and an unnamed prophet appears in Judges 6, but the book of Judges is dominated by military deliverers rather than by prophetic speech. The statement that visions were scarce captures a time when Israel's worship continued at Shiloh but direct communication from God was rare, partly, the text implies, because of the corruption of the priesthood.
cultural:
The lamp of God was the seven-branched lampstand in the sanctuary, which the priests were to keep burning from evening until morning (Exodus 27:20-21). Saying the lamp had not yet gone out places the call in the dark hours before dawn. The ark of the covenant, a gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the law, was the symbol of God's throne among his people, and Samuel sleeps in the temple where it was kept. Some interpreters think he slept in a room within the sanctuary complex rather than beside the ark itself, since only the high priest was to enter the most holy place, and the Hebrew allows either picture.

In the ancient world people widely believed gods communicated through dreams, and some sought revelations by sleeping in temples. What happens to Samuel is different: he isn't seeking anything, and the LORD comes and stands and calls him by name in words he mistakes for a human voice. The formula of verse 17, May God punish you, and ever so severely, was a standard oath that invoked a curse on the speaker if he failed to do what was required. Eli uses it to force Samuel to tell him the whole message.
literary: The chapter is built on a threefold pattern that turns on the fourth time. Three times the LORD calls, three times Samuel runs to Eli with “Here I am, for you have called me”, and three times Eli sends him back. The repetition creates suspense and a touch of humor, and it highlights both Samuel's readiness and his inexperience. Then Eli, whose eyes are failing and who has missed so much, sees what is happening and instructs the boy. The fourth call brings the message. The chapter is framed by statements about the word of the LORD: rare in verse 1, established in verses 19-21. Irony runs through it. The priest who cannot see is the one who recognizes God's voice, and the message the boy receives is judgment on the very man who taught him to listen. Eli's response in verse 18, “Let Him do what is good in His eyes”, is resigned acceptance, and readers debate whether it is humble faith or passive fatalism.

outline.t: A dark time: the word rare, Eli's eyes dim, the lamp still lit
The LORD calls Samuel four times
The message: judgment on Eli's house
Samuel tells Eli, and Eli accepts

doctrines.note: God makes himself known by his word. Samuel did not yet know the LORD, the text says, because the word had not yet been revealed to him. Knowing God, in this chapter, comes by God speaking and a person listening, and the LORD's revealing himself at Shiloh by his word marks a new era.

The judgment on Eli's house is confirmed. Eli is held responsible not only for his sons' sin but for failing to restrain them, a sober reminder that tolerating evil in one's care is itself a failure of faithfulness.

Samuel's answer, “Speak, for Your servant is listening” (verse 10), expresses the posture of faith: readiness to hear and obey, even before knowing what God will say. He then has the courage to pass on a hard message.

words.note: Davar, word, also thing or matter. The chapter is framed by the word of the LORD, rare at the start and established at the end. In Hebrew thought a word is not only information but something that happens; when God's word comes, it accomplishes what it says, and none of Samuel's words fall to the ground.

Qara, to call. It appears twelve times in the chapter, carrying the rhythm of the story. To be called by name in the Old Testament often marks a person for a particular task, as with Moses at the burning bush, where God also calls his name twice (Exodus 3:4).

Shama, to hear, which also means to listen and to obey. Samuel's answer uses this verb (your servant is listening), and the LORD warns of something at which the ears of all who hear will tingle. The book will repeatedly show that the difference between faithful and unfaithful leaders is whether they truly hear.

Chazon, vision. Verse 1 says visions were scarce, and verse 15 calls Samuel's experience a vision, though it is mostly heard rather than seen. The word came to be used for prophetic revelation in general, as in the opening line of Isaiah.

christ: The chapter shows God raising a prophet who stands between God and the people, hearing his word and speaking it faithfully, and who later anoints Israel's kings. The Old Testament promised a greater prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), and the New Testament presents Jesus as that prophet (Acts 3:22-24, where Peter mentions Samuel as one of the prophets who foretold these days). Where Samuel received the word of God, Jesus is described in John 1 as the Word himself, and Hebrews 1:1-2 contrasts God's speech in many ways through the prophets with his final speech through his Son. The parallel is a matter of pattern and fulfillment: Samuel is a true prophet in a dark time, and Christ is the one in whom God's speech reaches its fullness.

hard.q: Why does God say the iniquity of Eli's house will never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering?
hard.a: The statement sounds like an unforgivable sin, and readers find it troubling. In context, the sacrifices of the sanctuary are exactly what Eli's sons have abused and despised, and verse 14 says that the same system they profaned will not cover them. The judgment concerns the priestly family's office and its future; it is announced as a fixed decision because the warning of chapter 2 has gone unheeded. Interpreters differ on whether this shuts out individual repentance. Some read it as a judgment on the house as an institution, which does not decide the eternal state of each member. Others see it as similar to Old Testament statements about high-handed, defiant sin (Numbers 15:30-31), for which the sacrifices provided no remedy. Either way, the chapter's concern is the public judgment on a corrupt priesthood, and it presents that judgment as just.

questions: Samuel needed Eli's help to recognize God's voice. Who has helped you learn to hear God, and who might you help?
Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the vision. When have you had to deliver a hard truth to someone you respected, and what made it difficult?
The chapter begins with God's word rare and ends with it established. What would it mean for God's word to be less rare in your own life?
